# FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning

Haihui Pan    Junwei Bao    Hongfei Jiang    Yang Song
Affiliation: Zuoyebang Education Technology

###### Abstract

While large language models have made significant progress in
mathematical reasoning, they remain unreliable at judging the
correctness of their own solutions. Existing approaches that equip
models with self-verification typically treat solution generation and
verification as two separate tasks, leading to substantially increased
training time. In this paper, we propose FABSVer, which fuses these two
tasks into a single generation pass, dramatically reducing training
overhead while jointly optimizing both capabilities. We further identify
a convergence bottleneck both theoretically and empirically: as training
progresses, the reward reaches a plateau because the policy is
constrained by a fixed reference model. To overcome this, we introduce
Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU), which raises the reward ceiling
and enables sustained reward growth. Extensive experiments on math
benchmarks demonstrate that FABSVer achieves superior self-verification
and reasoning performance across three model scales, while requiring
only 51%–71% of the training time of existing methods. Analysis further
reveals distinct learning phases in how models acquire
self-verification, and that the gap between verify and answer rewards
shrinks noticeably as model size increases.

## 1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a foundational paradigm in
artificial intelligence, demonstrating remarkable capabilities across a
wide range of natural language processing tasks. Through scaling model
size, data, and compute, modern LLMs exhibit emergent abilities in code
generation, commonsense reasoning, and mathematical problem-solving
([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Jaech et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Team,
2024](#bib.bib3)). Among these, mathematical reasoning serves as a
critical benchmark for evaluating logical deduction and multi-step
inference, as it demands not only factual knowledge but also rigorous
step-by-step reasoning.

In recent years, LLMs have advanced substantially in mathematical
reasoning, largely driven by Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable
Rewards (RLVR) ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Zeng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10); [Jaech et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Hu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)). By leveraging objective, rule-based rewards derived
solely from final answer correctness, RLVR enables scalable training and
elicits sophisticated reasoning processes.

However, despite their improved problem-solving accuracy, LLMs trained
via RLVR suffer from a critical limitation: overconfidence in their own
outputs. As noted in recent studies, even when a generated solution is
fundamentally incorrect, the model frequently perceives it as correct
([Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Sareen
et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). This
verification gap motivates the need for self-verification—the ability of
a model to accurately judge the correctness of its own generated
sequences.

The importance of self-verification extends well beyond improved
accuracy. From a trustworthiness standpoint, LLM reasoning remains
largely opaque; self-verification offers a window into the model’s
confidence, helping users decide when to rely on its outputs and
enabling models to flag their own potential errors. Most fundamentally,
from a comprehension perspective, solving a problem without the ability
to judge the correctness of a solution reflects, at best, a superficial
understanding. Just as true mastery entails evaluating both one’s own
answers and those of others, genuine reasoning requires the integration
of generation and verification.

Recent work on intrinsic self-verification, such as RISE ([Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2)), jointly optimizes solution generation and
verification during online reinforcement learning. However, these
approaches treat generation and verification as two independent forward
passes. Given $`N`$ questions, with $`k`$ solutions generated per
question and $`m`$ verification judgments per solution, the total number
of forward passes inflates from $`N\cdot k`$ to $`N\cdot k\cdot(1+m)`$,
multiplicatively increasing both training data and inference time. This
overhead makes large-scale self-verification training prohibitively
expensive.

Beyond training efficiency, a more fundamental challenge stems from the
optimization dynamics of RLVR itself. In standard frameworks such as PPO
and GRPO ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib9); [Shao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12)), a fixed reference model regularizes policy updates
via a KL divergence penalty. While this stabilizes training, it imposes
an implicit upper bound on policy improvement: as we theoretically
demonstrate, once the KL divergence ceases to grow, the achievable
reward is effectively capped. This bottleneck is particularly
detrimental for self-verification training, which requires sustained
exploration over extended horizons.

To address these challenges, we propose FABSVer (Faster Training and
Better Self-Verification), built upon two key innovations: (1) Task
Fusion, which merges solution generation and self-verification into a
single forward pass, eliminating the multiplicative overhead; and (2)
Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU), which periodically resets the
reference model to the current policy, releasing the KL constraint and
enabling sustained reward growth. We provide theoretical justification
for DRMU by deriving an upper bound relating the expected reward to the
KL divergence.

We validate FABSVer on three model scales (1.5B, 3B, and 7B) across
multiple math benchmarks. The results, detailed in
Section [5](#S5 "5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"),
show that FABSVer consistently outperforms existing methods in both
self-verification and reasoning, while requiring substantially less
training time. Beyond performance gains, our analysis uncovers new
insights into the training dynamics of self-verification.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

- •
  We propose FABSVer, a task-fused training framework that unifies
  solution generation and self-verification into a single forward pass,
  eliminating the multiplicative overhead of existing approaches while
  enabling synergistic optimization of both capabilities.
- •
  We introduce DRMU, a simple yet theoretically grounded mechanism that
  overcomes the convergence bottleneck caused by a fixed reference
  model, enabling sustained reward growth with theoretical guarantees.
- •
  Through extensive experiments across three model scales, we
  demonstrate that FABSVer achieves superior performance at
  substantially lower training cost, and we uncover distinct learning
  phases and scaling effects in self-verification acquisition.

## 2 Related work

#### RLVR for Reasoning.

Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has recently
emerged as a powerful paradigm for enhancing LLM reasoning capabilities
([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Zeng et al., 2025](#bib.bib10); [Jaech
et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib17)). Unlike
previous RL approaches that rely on either human preference annotations
([Ouyang et al., 2022](#bib.bib13); [Rafailov et al., 2023](#bib.bib14))
or complex process reward models that require fine-grained supervision
([Lightman et al., 2023](#bib.bib5); [Setlur et al., 2024](#bib.bib16)),
RLVR leverages objective, rule-based rewards derived solely from final
answer correctness, such as exact match with ground truth or passing
unit tests. This key advantage—providing feedback based only on the
final output without requiring complete output annotations or dense
signals from process supervision—enables scalable and efficient training
for reasoning tasks. Recent works ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Zeng
et al., 2025](#bib.bib10); [Jaech et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [Hu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib17)) have demonstrated that such outcome-based RL can
effectively elicit sophisticated reasoning processes in LLMs, achieving
substantial improvements on mathematical and programming benchmarks.

#### Self-Verification for LLM.

Self-verification—the ability of a model to evaluate the correctness of
its own outputs—has been recognized as a crucial capability for reliable
LLM reasoning ([Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Sareen et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19); [Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)). While RLVR
effectively improves a model’s problem-solving accuracy through
outcome-based rewards, recent studies have identified a notable
limitation: models trained with RLVR often lack robust self-verification
capabilities ([Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Sareen et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)). Specifically, these models tend to exhibit
overconfidence, incorrectly judging their own erroneous solutions as
correct. This observation has motivated a growing body of research aimed
at equipping models with both problem-solving and self-verification
abilities simultaneously ([Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). By jointly
optimizing for solution generation and correctness verification, these
approaches seek to address the verification gap and further enhance the
reliability of LLM reasoning systems.

## 3 Preliminaries

### 3.1 Reinforcement Learning for LLMs

Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial technique for
aligning LLMs with human preferences and specific task objectives. In
the context of LLMs, the RL framework is adapted as follows: the policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ is the language model itself, parameterized by
$`\theta`$, which generates text autoregressively. At each generation
step $`t`$, given a prompt x and previously generated tokens
$`\textbf{y}_{<t}`$, the model produces a next token $`y_{t}`$ according
to $`\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|\textbf{x},\textbf{y}_{<t})`$. The complete
response $`\textbf{y}=(y_{1},y_{2},...,y_{|\textbf{y}|})`$ forms a
trajectory. After generating the complete response, a reward model or
task-specific metric assigns a scalar reward $`r`$ reflecting the
overall quality of the response.

#### Policy gradient (PG).

PG methods ([Sutton et al., 1999](#bib.bib21)) provide a way to optimize
the language model directly by estimating the gradient of the expected
reward. For LLMs, the standard policy gradient objective can be written
as:

|     |                                                                                                                 |                                                      |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{PG}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\textbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D},\textbf{y}\sim\pi\_{\theta}(\cdot | \textbf{x})}\left[r(\textbf{x},\textbf{y})\right],`$ |     | (1) |

where $`\mathcal{D}`$ is the input distribution and
$`r(\textbf{x},\textbf{y})`$ is the reward for response y given input x.

#### Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO).

PPO ([Schulman et al., 2017](#bib.bib9)) was originally designed to
improve training stability by restricting policy updates to a trust
region. In the context of LLMs, the objective of PPO is typically
formulated as maximizing a clipped surrogate objective while
incorporating a KL-divergence penalty to keep the learned policy close
to a reference model $`\pi_{\text{ref}}`$:

|     |                                                                                                                             |                             |            |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------- | ---------- | -------------- | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{PPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\textbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D},\textbf{y}\sim\pi\_{\text{old}}(\cdot | \textbf{x})}\left[\frac{1}{ | \textbf{y} | }\sum\_{t=1}^{ | \textbf{y} | }\min\left(r*{t}(\theta)\hat{A}*{t},\text{clip}(r*{t}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}*{t}\right)-\beta\text{KL}[\pi\_{\theta} |     | \pi\_{\text{ref}}]\right],`$ |     | (2) |

where
$`r_{t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{t}|\textbf{x},\textbf{y}_{<t})}{\pi_{\text{old}}(y_{t}|\textbf{x},\textbf{y}_{<t})}`$
is the importance sampling ratio, $`\hat{A}_{t}`$ is the advantage
estimate, and $`\beta`$ is a coefficient controlling the strength of the
KL penalty. PPO relies on a value model to compute advantages, which
introduces significant memory and computational overhead during
training.

#### Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

To eliminate the need for an expensive value model, GRPO ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib8)) introduces a novel group-based advantage estimation
method. For the same input x, GRPO first samples a group of $`G`$
outputs $`\{\textbf{y}_{1},\textbf{y}_{2},\dots,\textbf{y}_{G}\}`$ from
the old policy $`\pi_{\text{old}}`$. Instead of learning a value model,
it estimates the advantage by comparing rewards within this group. For
each output $`\textbf{y}_{i}`$, we obtain its reward score
$`r_{i}=r(\textbf{x},\textbf{y}_{i})`$ from the reward model. The
advantage $`\hat{A}_{i}`$ for the $`i`$-th output is defined as the
reward normalized by the mean and standard deviation of the group. The
optimization objective of GRPO is then formulated as:

|     |                                                     |                                                                                                                                                                                       |                |                                     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------- | ----------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)=`$ | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\textbf{x}\sim\mathcal{D},\{\textbf{y}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot                                                                           | \textbf{x})}`$ |                                     |     |
|     |                                                     | $`\displaystyle\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum*{i=1}^{G}\left(\min\left(r*{i}(\theta)\hat{A}_{i},\text{clip}(r_{i}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\hat{A}_{i}\right)-\beta\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta} |                | \pi\_{\text{ref}}]\right)\right],`$ |     | (3) |

where
$`r_{i}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(\textbf{y}|\textbf{x})}{\pi_{\text{old}}(\textbf{y}|\textbf{x})}`$
is the importance sampling ratio and
$`\hat{A}_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\text{mean}(r_{1},\cdots,r_{G})}{\text{std}(r_{1},\cdots,r_{G})}`$.

### 3.2 Self-Verification for LLMs

Recent studies indicate that LLMs trained via RVLR often suffer from
overconfidence regarding their generated outputs y. Even when the
generated solution y is fundamentally incorrect, the model frequently
perceives it as correct ([Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib2); [Sareen et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)). The primary goal of self-verification is to endow
the policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ with the capability to accurately judge the
correctness of its own generated sequence y.

To develop this self-verification capability, existing approaches
typically joint-train two tasks during the reinforcement learning phase:
solution generation and solution verification ([Shao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Sareen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib18); [Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). Specifically,
given an input question x, the policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ first generates a
solution y. Subsequently, conditioned on x, y, and a specialized
self-verification prompt $`I_{v}`$, the policy produces a verification
outcome v. For verifiable mathematical problems, the reward for solution
generation can be straightforwardly derived via rule-based evaluation,
checking whether the generated answer y matches the ground-truth
$`\textbf{y}^{*}`$. Likewise, the reward signal for the verification
task can also be determined using rule-based logic based on the triplet
$`(\textbf{v},\textbf{y},\textbf{y}^{*})`$. For instance, when the
verification output v asserts that the generated solution is correct, a
true reward is obtained by checking whether y is indeed consistent with
$`\textbf{y}^{*}`$.

Therefore, the overall optimization objective for these methods
integrates the RL objectives of both generation and verification, which
can be formulated as:

|     |                                                                                                                                          |                                                                                                            |                                                                                                           |
| --- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{SV}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{(\textbf{x},\textbf{y}^{\*})\sim\mathcal{D},\textbf{y}\sim\pi\_{\theta}(\cdot | \textbf{x})}\left[r*{\text{gen}}(\textbf{y},\textbf{y}^{\*})+\mathbb{E}*{\textbf{v}\sim\pi\_{\theta}(\cdot | \textbf{x},\textbf{y},I*{v})}\left[r*{\text{ver}}(\textbf{v},\textbf{y},\textbf{y}^{\*})\right]\right],`$ |     | (4) |

where $`\mathcal{D}`$ denotes the dataset containing questions x and
their corresponding ground-truth answers $`\textbf{y}^{*}`$;
$`r_{\text{gen}}`$ and $`r_{\text{ver}}`$ are the rule-based reward
functions for the solution generation and verification tasks,
respectively.

The fundamental difference between ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) and
([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)) lies in the formalization of the
verification prompt $`I_{v}`$. While ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2))
treats the self-verification query as a completely independent,
standalone prompt, ([Zhang et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)) structures it as a
follow-up query within a multi-turn conversation (i.e., a second-turn
request). The $`I_{v}`$ of these two methods are shown in
[Figure 4](#A5.F4 "In Appendix E Verification Prompt in Related Approaches ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")
and
[Figure 5](#A5.F5 "In Appendix E Verification Prompt in Related Approaches ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"),
respectively. ([Shao et al., 2025](#bib.bib12)) uses human-annotated
data to train Verification and Meta-Verification, which provide feedback
for solution generation and solution verification. Subsequently, RL is
used to train the policy’s ability to generate solutions and its
self-verification capability.

## 4 Faster Training and Better Self-Verification (FABSVer)

Existing methods for self-verification treat solution generation and
verification as two separate tasks, performing independent forward
passes for each during online RL training. Given $`N`$ questions with
$`k`$ solutions per question and $`m`$ verification judgments per
solution, the total number of forward passes expands from $`N\cdot k`$
to $`N\cdot k\cdot(1+m)`$, multiplicatively increasing both training
data and inference time. This prohibitive overhead stems from a
fundamental design choice: the decoupling of generation and
verification.

#### Motivation and Core Idea.

To address this, we propose FABSVer, which fuses solution generation and
self-verification into a single forward pass, eliminating the
multiplicative overhead. To further address the convergence bottleneck
caused by the fixed reference model, we introduce DRMU, which
periodically resets the reference model to the current policy, releasing
the KL constraint and enabling sustained reward growth.

Due to space constraints, we defer the algorithm overview to
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Algorithm Overview ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning").
The overall procedure of FABSVer is summarized in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix C Algorithm Overview ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"):
each generation produces both the solution and the verification result
in a single forward pass, optimizes with the combined reward
$`r_{\text{combine}}`$, and periodically updates the reference model.

### 4.1 Task Fusion and Reward Design

Task Fusion. To reduce training overhead, we propose to output both the
solution and the self-verification result in a single generation.
Specifically, given an input $`\mathbf{x}`$, the model $`\pi_{\theta}`$
generates a solution $`\mathbf{y}`$ and a verification result
$`\mathbf{v}`$ in one forward pass. The prompt template used for
training and inference is shown in
[Figure 3](#A4.F3 "In Appendix D Prompt for training and inference ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"),
where the model is instructed to output the reasoning process, answer,
and verification result within $`<\texttt{think}>`$,
$`<\texttt{answer}>`$, and $`<\texttt{verify}>`$ tags, respectively.
Compared with existing methods, the training data size does not incur
additional increase, and no second forward pass is required for
verification, thereby significantly reducing training time and
computational cost.

Reward Design. Under the single-generation framework, we redesign the
reward function. We introduce three binary reward signals based on the
format, the solution, and the verification result:
$`r_{\text{format}}(\mathbf{y})\in\{0,1\}`$ indicates whether the output
format is correct,
$`r_{\text{gen}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}^{*})\in\{0,1\}`$ indicates
whether the generated solution $`\mathbf{y}`$ matches the ground truth
$`\mathbf{y}^{*}`$, and
$`r_{\text{ver}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{y}^{*})\in\{0,1\}`$
indicates whether the verification result $`\mathbf{v}`$ correctly
judges the solution. The final combined reward
$`r_{\text{combine}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{y}^{*})`$ is then
defined as:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle r*{\text{combine}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{y}^{\*})=\begin{cases}1.0,&\text{if }r*{\text{format}}(\mathbf{y})=1\text{ and }r*{\text{gen}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}^{\*})=1\text{ and }r*{\text{ver}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{y}^{\*})=1\\[4.0pt] |

0.5,&\text{if }r*{\text{format}}(\mathbf{y})=1\text{ and }r*{\text{gen}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}^{_})=1\text{ and }r\_{\text{ver}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{y}^{_})=0\\[4.0pt]
0.25,&\text{if }r*{\text{format}}(\mathbf{y})=1\text{ and }r*{\text{gen}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{y}^{_})=0\text{ and }r\_{\text{ver}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{y}^{_})=1\\[4.0pt]
0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}`$ | | (5) |

Design Principles: The design of
$`r_{\text{combine}}(\mathbf{y},\mathbf{v},\mathbf{y}^{*})`$ follows
three principles.

1.  1.  Reward for correct solutions is significantly higher than for
        incorrect ones: A correct solution with correct verification
        receives the highest reward (1.0), a correct solution with incorrect
        verification receives a medium reward (0.5), while an incorrect
        solution can receive at most 0.25 (only if the verification is
        correct). This reflects the consideration that solution generation
        is more difficult than self-verification.
2.  2.  Encourage correct self-verification: Even if the solution is
        incorrect, a correct verification still receives a small positive
        reward (0.25) to guide the model to learn accurate judgment of its
        own output. If both the solution and the verification are incorrect,
        the reward is zero.
3.  3.  Both correct solution and correct verification are required for the
        highest reward: The model must improve both its generation ability
        and its self-verification ability simultaneously to achieve optimal
        performance.

Additional Advantages of Task Fusion. Beyond reducing training overhead,
task fusion brings two additional advantages:

- •
  Flexible output control. In practice, the $`<\texttt{verify}>`$ tag
  can be treated as an EOS (End of Sequence) token, allowing the model
  to flexibly decide whether to output the verification result on demand
  without any architectural modification.
- •
  Joint optimization effect. In the two-task framework, generation and
  verification are optimized independently by $`r_{\text{gen}}`$ and
  $`r_{\text{ver}}`$ respectively; verification errors do not affect the
  reward for generation. In contrast, under the fused framework, the
  combined reward $`r_{\text{combine}}`$ depends on both the correctness
  of the solution and the correctness of the verification. For example,
  even if the solution is correct, a wrong verification reduces the
  total reward from 1.0 to 0.5. This coupling mechanism encourages the
  model to improve its self-verification ability while optimizing
  generation, as verification errors directly reduce the overall reward,
  thereby providing a stronger joint learning signal.

### 4.2 Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU)

Although task fusion significantly reduces training overhead, during RL
training we observe that the reward increases slowly in the later stage,
while the KL divergence barely increases. This indicates that the policy
update is constrained by the fixed reference model $`\pi_{\text{ref}}`$.
Intuitively, while the KL divergence provides stability for policy
updates, it also acts as a constraint that limits exploration. We
further analyze this phenomenon theoretically in
[Theorem 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 4.1. ‣ 4.2 Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU) ‣ 4 Faster Training and Better Self-Verification (FABSVer) ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning").
The proof of
[Theorem 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 4.1. ‣ 4.2 Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU) ‣ 4 Faster Training and Better Self-Verification (FABSVer) ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")
can be found in the Appendix
 [F](#A6 "Appendix F Proof of ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning").

###### Theorem 4.1.

Let $`\pi_{\theta}(y|x)`$ be the policy to be optimized, and
$`\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)`$ be the reference model. For every reward model
$`r(x,y)`$ such that
$`\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}[e^{r(x,y)}]<\infty`$, then we have:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}[r(x,y)]\leq\mathrm{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]+\log\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}[e^{r(x,y)}]
``` |  |

In RL algorithms such as PPO or GRPO, $`\pi_{\text{ref}}`$ is fixed, and
thus the second term on the right-hand side of the inequality is
constant. Consequently, if $`\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]`$
no longer increases, the upper bound of the reward becomes locked,
making further improvement difficult.

To break this limitation, we propose Dynamic Reference Model Update
(DRMU). Specifically, at certain epochs or training steps, we replace
the reference model $`\pi_{\text{ref}}`$ with the current policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$. This operation resets
$`\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]`$ to 0, allowing the policy
to regain room to diverge from the reference model (i.e., releasing the
KL budget), thereby enabling continued reward optimization. Meanwhile,
the updated reference model is closer to the current policy, which helps
maintain training stability. In this way, DRMU effectively accelerates
the overall convergence process.

## 5 Experiment

### 5.1 Setup

#### Models, Dataset and Training Details.

We follow the same experimental setup as ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2))
for both training data and model selection. We use three Qwen2.5 base
models ([Team, 2024](#bib.bib3)) of varying sizes—1.5B, 3B, and 7B—for
our experiments, and MATH-Hard (Level 3–5) ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib4)) serves as the training set throughout. Due to space
constraints, the training details are provided in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Training Details. ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning").

#### Benchmarks and Evaluation.

We evaluate our models on five mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
MATH500 ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib4); [Lightman et al.,
2023](#bib.bib5)), a subset of the MATH test set, serves as an
in-distribution test to assess the efficacy of learning. To evaluate
out-of-distribution generalization, we use OlympiadBench([He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib7)), AIME2024, AMC2023 and Minerva ([Lewkowycz et al.,
2022](#bib.bib6)). Among these, AIME2024 and Olympiad feature
competition-level problems, allowing us to rigorously assess model
performance on challenging, multi-step reasoning tasks. Following the
evaluation setup in ([Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)), we generate 8
responses per problem with a sampling temperature of 1 and adopt Pass@1
([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib11)) accuracy as our primary metric.
Specifically, reasoning correctness is determined by the final answer in
the model’s response, and verification correctness is assessed based on
both the model’s predicted verification result and its consistency with
the gold answer. To ensure reproducibility of the results, we use the
same inference seed for all models.

### 5.2 Comparative Analysis of Self-Verification and Reasoning Performance

Experimental results on self-verification and reasoning performance are
reported in
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Comparative Analysis of Self-Verification and Reasoning Performance ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"),
while training efficiency comparisons are provided in
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Comparative Analysis of Self-Verification and Reasoning Performance ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning").

From Base to FABSVer, the model exhibits a pronounced dual-improvement
trend in both self-verification and reasoning capabilities. As shown in
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Comparative Analysis of Self-Verification and Reasoning Performance ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"),
taking Qwen2.5-1.5B as an example, the average self-verification score
surges from 20.2% to 79.8%, while the average reasoning score rises from
1.1% to 26.6%, indicating that FABSVer achieves positive synergistic
gains in both capabilities without sacrificing reasoning performance for
self-verification accuracy. This dual-improvement trend holds
consistently across the 3B and 7B model sizes, demonstrating the strong
scalability of the proposed method.

In stark contrast, Zero-RL focuses predominantly on enhancing reasoning
performance but yields only marginal improvements in self-verification.
For the 1.5B model, Zero-RL attains a reasoning average of 24.0%, a
substantial gain over the Base score of 1.1%; however, its
self-verification average reaches merely 26.8%, far below the 79.8%
achieved by FABSVer. This “one-sided improvement” phenomenon persists
across both the 3B and 7B models. These results indicate that
reasoning-oriented training alone cannot spontaneously engender
high-quality self-verification capability. FABSVer, by contrast,
successfully realizes synergistic gains in both capacities—substantially
raising the ceiling of self-verification while maintaining a lead in
reasoning performance.

FABSVer also comprehensively outperforms the concurrent work RISE across
both dimensions, with demonstrably lower training costs. As detailed in
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Comparative Analysis of Self-Verification and Reasoning Performance ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"),
FABSVer surpasses RISE in self-verification by 5.3%, 2.7%, and 4.5% on
the 1.5B, 3B, and 7B models, respectively. In terms of reasoning,
FABSVer likewise maintains a consistent advantage over RISE across all
three model sizes, confirming that the enhanced self-verification
capability does not come at the expense of reasoning performance.
Crucially, with respect to training efficiency,
Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Comparative Analysis of Self-Verification and Reasoning Performance ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")
shows that the training time of FABSVer amounts to only 51% to 71% of
that required by RISE, representing a Pareto improvement of stronger
performance with lower computational overhead. This comprehensive
superiority substantiates that FABSVer, through a more streamlined
training paradigm, achieves synergistic advancement in both
error-detection and reasoning capabilities.

### 5.3 Ablation Study

To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed Dynamic Reference Model
Update (DRMU), we conduct ablation experiments on FABSVer by removing
DRMU while keeping all other components unchanged. Both quantitative
results on math benchmarks and training dynamics are analyzed.

#### Quantitative Results.

Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Training Dynamics. ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")
presents the ablation results across 1.5B, 3B, and 7B model sizes.
Overall, DRMU brings consistent improvements in both self-verification
and reasoning capabilities. In terms of self-verification, FABSVer with
DRMU outperforms its counterpart without DRMU by 1.7%, 6.2%, and 2.6% on
average for the 1.5B, 3B, and 7B models, respectively. The gains are
particularly pronounced on challenging competition-level benchmarks such
as AIME and OlympiadBench, demonstrating that DRMU effectively enhances
the model’s error-detection ability on difficult problems. In terms of
reasoning, DRMU also yields consistent improvements across all three
model sizes, confirming that the enhanced self-verification capability
does not come at the cost of reasoning performance.

#### Training Dynamics.

Figure [1](#S5.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Training Dynamics. ‣ 5.3 Ablation Study ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")
illustrates the training curves of combined reward and KL divergence for
FABSVer with and without DRMU. For the variant with DRMU, the reference
model is updated at steps 273, 546, and 819, which correspond to epochs
4, 8, and 12, respectively. After each update, the KL divergence drops
sharply to approximately zero, since the current policy becomes the new
reference. This KL reset releases the constraint imposed by the fixed
reference model, allowing the policy to continue exploring and improving
its reward. As a result, FABSVer with DRMU achieves higher final rewards
across all three model sizes compared to the variant without DRMU.

In contrast, without DRMU, the KL divergence ceases to exhibit
significant growth in the later stages of training, and the reward
improvement decelerates accordingly. This observation aligns with
[Theorem 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 4.1. ‣ 4.2 Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU) ‣ 4 Faster Training and Better Self-Verification (FABSVer) ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning").
Consequently, when $`\mathrm{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]`$ stops
increasing, the ceiling on the achievable reward is effectively capped,
limiting the potential for further improvement. By periodically
resetting the KL to zero, DRMU raises this ceiling and thus enables
continued reward growth.

### 5.4 Analysis of Answer and Verify Rewards during Training

Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.4 Analysis of Answer and Verify Rewards during Training ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")
presents the training curves of answer reward and verify reward for
FABSVer across three model sizes. Several notable patterns emerge from
these dynamics.

In the early stages of training, the answer reward and verify reward are
nearly identical across all model sizes. We observe that the model
exhibits a strong tendency to always predict its own outputs as correct
at this stage. This can be attributed to a free-riding effect: as the
model’s answer generation capability steadily improves, it produces
correct answers with increasing frequency. Consequently, the verify task
can achieve a steadily increasing reward by simply predicting “Correct”
for every sample, without developing any genuine discriminative ability.
As a result, the verify reward passively tracks the answer reward, and
the two remain tightly coupled.

As training progresses into the middle and later stages, the growth of
answer reward decelerates. At this point, the free-riding strategy
becomes insufficient—merely judging most outputs as correct no longer
yields additional reward gains. To further improve the overall reward,
the model is forced to develop the ability to correctly identify its own
errors. This shift from a naive “almost-always-correct” strategy to a
more sophisticated discriminative policy drives a second wave of verify
reward improvement, allowing it to outpace answer reward. This
phenomenon represents a forced learning effect: the model must learn to
discriminate in order to unlock further reward when answer quality
plateaus.

Notably, the gap between verify reward and answer reward shrinks as
model size increases. For smaller models (e.g., 1.5B), verify reward
notably surpasses answer reward, reflecting their greater reliance on
explicit verification learning. For larger models (e.g., 7B), the gap
between the two rewards is considerably smaller, suggesting that larger
models possess stronger intrinsic self-verification capabilities—likely
acquired during pretraining—and thus require less explicit
discriminative training to achieve relatively balanced performance. This
observation is consistent with the results in
Table [1](#S5.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 5.2 Comparative Analysis of Self-Verification and Reasoning Performance ‣ 5 Experiment ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"),
where larger models consistently achieve higher absolute
self-verification scores.

Figure 2: Training curves of answer reward and verify reward for FABSVer
across different model sizes.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose FABSVer, a streamlined training paradigm that
fuses solution generation and self-verification into a single forward
pass, substantially reducing training overhead while achieving
synergistic gains in both capabilities. Through a combined reward design
and the Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU) mechanism, FABSVer
overcomes the convergence bottleneck imposed by a fixed reference model,
enabling sustained reward growth. Our experimental results demonstrate
that FABSVer consistently outperforms existing methods across multiple
model sizes and math benchmarks, achieving stronger performance with
lower computational cost. Further analysis of training dynamics reveals
that models undergo a two-phase transition in acquiring
self-verification ability—from an early free-riding stage to a later
forced learning stage.

## Appendix A Limitation

The trained LLM, although capable of serving as a rule verifier to guide
RL training on unlabeled data for self-improvement, is not explored in
this direction within this paper and remains future work. Meanwhile, the
training data in this work are entirely derived from mathematical
reasoning tasks; despite the model exhibiting a certain degree of
generalization ability, its effectiveness in broader domains beyond
those with verifiable rewards still requires further validation. In
addition, we primarily adopt final inference accuracy as the evaluation
metric. However, a single metric makes it difficult to fully capture the
criticality of the model’s emergent verification behavior, indicating
that the evaluation system still needs further refinement.

## Appendix B Training Details.

We use trl \[[von Werra et al., 2020](#bib.bib22)\] for our experiments.
During RL training, the training batch size is set to 1024, with a
constant learning rate of 5e-7 and a uniform KL penalty coefficient of
1e-2. The sampling temperature is set to 1.0, and we roll out 8
responses per problem. The maximum output length is set to 3000 tokens.
We train for 16 epochs, and the reference model is updated every 4
epochs. As the Qwen2.5-1.5B Base and Qwen2.5-3B Base models have
difficulty producing responses in the required format, we first sample
5K correct responses from the Qwen2.5-7B Base model’s training run and
use them to fine-tune the 1.5B and 3B models for 20 steps, before
proceeding with RL training on these two models.

## Appendix C Algorithm Overview

Input Language model $`\pi_{\theta_{\text{init}}}`$; dataset
$`\mathcal{D}`$; number of solutions per question $`K`$; generation
batch size $`\mathcal{B}_{g}`$; total training iterations $`N`$;
reference model update interval $`U`$.

1: Initialize: policy
$`\pi_{\theta}\leftarrow\pi_{\theta_{\text{init}}}`$, reference model
$`\pi_{\text{ref}}\leftarrow\pi_{\theta_{\text{init}}}`$

2: for $`\text{iteration}=1`$ to $`N`$ do

3:   Sample $`\mathcal{B}_{g}`$ questions
$`\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i}^{*})\}_{i=1}^{\mathcal{B}_{g}}\sim\mathcal{D}`$

4:   Generate solutions and verification results in a single forward
pass: $`\triangleright`$ Task Fusion

5:   
$`\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{\text{train}}\leftarrow\bigl\{(\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{y}_{i}^{(k)},\mathbf{v}_{i}^{(k)},r_{\text{combine}}(\mathbf{y}_{i}^{(k)},\mathbf{v}_{i}^{(k)},\mathbf{y}_{i}^{*}))\,\bigm|\,(\mathbf{y}_{i}^{(k)},\mathbf{v}_{i}^{(k)})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|\mathbf{x}_{i}),\,i\leq\mathcal{B}_{g},\,k\leq K\bigr\}`$

6:   Compute rewards using
Eq. [5](#S4.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 4.1 Task Fusion and Reward Design ‣ 4 Faster Training and Better Self-Verification (FABSVer) ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")

7:   Update policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ using GRPO objective
(Eq. [3](#S3.Ex1 "In Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). ‣ 3.1 Reinforcement Learning for LLMs ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning"))
with reference model $`\pi_{\text{ref}}`$

8:   if $`\text{iteration}\bmod U=0`$ then $`\triangleright`$ Dynamic
Reference Model Update

9:    $`\pi_{\text{ref}}\leftarrow\pi_{\theta}`$

10:   end if

11: end for

Output Optimized policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$

Algorithm 1 FABSVer (GRPO)

## Appendix F Proof of [Theorem 4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 4.1. ‣ 4.2 Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU) ‣ 4 Faster Training and Better Self-Verification (FABSVer) ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")

See
[4.1](#S4.Thmtheorem1 "Theorem 4.1. ‣ 4.2 Dynamic Reference Model Update (DRMU) ‣ 4 Faster Training and Better Self-Verification (FABSVer) ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")

###### Proof.

We can construct a Gibbs distribution $`\pi_{\phi}(y|x)`$ based on
$`\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)`$ and $`r(x,y)`$ as follows:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\pi_{\phi}(y|x)=\frac{e^{r(x,y)}}{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}[e^{r(x,y)}]}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x).`$ |  | (6) |

Furthermore, we can obtain:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}{\pi_{\phi}(y|x)}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}[e^{r(x,y)}]}{e^{r(x,y)}}.`$ |  | (7) |

Now, let us compute the KL divergence between $`\pi_{\theta}(y|x)`$ and
$`\pi_{\phi}(y|x)`$:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\phi}]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}{\pi_{\phi}(y|x)}\right]=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}\left[\log\left(\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}\cdot\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}{\pi_{\phi}(y|x)}\right)\right]`$ |  | (8) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]+\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}\left[\log\frac{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}{\pi_{\phi}(y|x)}\right].`$ |  | (9) |

Substituting
Eq. [7](#A6.E7 "Equation 7 ‣ Proof. ‣ Appendix F Proof of ‣ FABSVer: Faster Training and Better Self-Verification for LLM Mathematical Reasoning")
into the above expression yields:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\phi}]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]+\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}\left[\log\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}[e^{r(x,y)}]}{e^{r(x,y)}}\right]`$ |  | (10) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]+\log\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}[e^{r(x,y)}]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}[r(x,y)].`$ |  | (11) |

By the non-negativity of KL divergence, we have
$`\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\phi}]\geq 0`$. Therefore, we can finally
prove:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta}(y|x)}[r(x,y)]\leq\text{KL}[\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}]+\log\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y|x)}[e^{r(x,y)}].`$ |  | (12) |

∎
````
